entry.sum: To compare two groups, match their things one to one or count them: the group with things left over has more. Numbers later in the counting list are greater, and we record comparisons with $>$, $<$ and $=$. Whole numbers are compared by place value: more digits means greater, otherwise the highest place where the digits differ decides.
entry.why: Comparing and ordering is how children first meet the order of the numbers, which later becomes position on the number line and the inequalities of algebra.

blocks.body:
This page is about two questions. Which is more? And how do we put numbers in order?

We start with real things: two groups of objects, matched or counted. Then we compare the numbers 1 to 10, learn the words and the symbols $>$, $<$ and $=$, and finish with big numbers such as 547,612, where the places of the digits do the work.

You need to be able to count a group of things and say how many there are (see [[counting-number-names]]). Later sections use tens and ones; the page on [[place-value]] explains them fully.

blocks.title: More, fewer or the same: comparing two groups
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to say which of two groups has more things, which has fewer, or whether they have the same number.

Try this first. Four children sit at a table. There are three erasers. Is there an eraser for every child? Hand out the erasers, one to each child, and see what happens.

Every child who gets an eraser makes a pair: one child, one eraser. When the erasers run out, one child is still waiting. So there are not enough erasers. There are more children than erasers, and fewer erasers than children.

blocks.title: More, fewer, the same
blocks.body:
Match the things in two groups one to one: each thing in the first group gets a partner from the second group, and no thing is used twice.

- If every thing has a partner and nothing is left over, the two groups have the same number. We also say they are equal.
- If some things are left over in one group, that group has more. The other group has fewer.

The English curriculum asks children to use the words equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most and least.

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(5.4, 2.6); ax = plt.gca()
xs = [0, 1.5, 3, 4.5]
for x in xs:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x, 2.0), 0.35, fill=False, ec='black', lw=1.4))
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x, 2.0), 0.06, color='black'))
for x in xs[:3]:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x - 0.4, 0.25), 0.8, 0.5, fc='#cfe0ff', ec='blue', lw=1.4))
    ax.plot([x, x], [1.62, 0.78], color='black', lw=1.2)
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((4.5, 2.0), 0.55, fill=False, ec='red', lw=1.4, ls='--'))
ax.text(4.5, 0.5, 'no eraser', color='red', ha='center', va='center')
ax.text(-0.75, 2.0, 'children', ha='right', va='center')
ax.text(-0.75, 0.5, 'erasers', ha='right', va='center')
ax.set_xlim(-3.0, 5.4); ax.set_ylim(0.0, 2.7); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 4 children and 3 erasers. Each line pairs one eraser with one child. 3 pairs are made and 1 child is left over, so there are more children than erasers.
blocks.alt: Top row: four circles standing for children. Bottom row: three blue rectangles standing for erasers. Three lines join the first three children to the three erasers. The fourth child has a red dashed ring and the words no eraser.

blocks.title: Ways to compare two groups
blocks.body: Each way below gives the same answer. Children use whichever fits the things in front of them.

items.label: Matching
items.body: Give each thing a partner from the other group, one to one, and look for leftovers. This needs no counting at all.

items.label: Counting
items.body: Count each group. The group with the number that comes later when you count has more. With 9 milk and 5 water, fewer chose water, because 5 comes before 9.

items.label: Towers side by side
items.body: Build a tower of cubes for each group and stand the towers next to each other. The taller tower (with cubes the same size) has more.

items.label: Make them equal
items.body: Ask what would make the groups the same. One bag has 6 apples and another has 2. Moving apples until both bags hold 4 shows the first bag had more.

blocks.title: Number, not size
blocks.body: When we compare how many, only the number of things matters. A big thing and a small thing each count as one.

Matching pairs one thing with one thing. A big ball can be paired with a small marble just as well as with another ball. So the size of the things never changes which group has leftovers. In the picture below, match each ball with a marble: 3 pairs, and 2 marbles are left over. There are more marbles, even though the balls take up more room.

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(5.4, 2.4); ax = plt.gca()
for i in range(3):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0.8 + 1.7 * i, 1.0), 0.7, fc='#ffe0b8', ec='orange', lw=1.4))
for i in range(5):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((6.6 + 0.7 * i, 1.0), 0.22, fc='#d8f0d8', ec='green', lw=1.4))
ax.text(2.5, -0.25, '3 big balls', ha='center', va='top')
ax.text(8.0, -0.25, '5 small marbles', ha='center', va='top')
ax.plot([5.6, 5.6], [0.0, 2.0], color='black', lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 10.0); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 2.0); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 3 big balls and 5 small marbles. The marbles are smaller, but there are more of them: 5 is more than 3.
blocks.alt: Left: three large orange circles labelled 3 big balls. Right, after a dividing line: five small green circles labelled 5 small marbles.

blocks.title: For adults: more is not bigger
blocks.body: Young children often judge more by size: the pile that looks bigger must have more. The NCETM suggests starting with groups whose numbers are very different, then giving collections with many small things and few large things, so the child has to think about how many rather than how big. Include some groups that are equal, and always ask how do you know? and can you check by matching or counting?
There are 6 apples and 5 plates. Are there more apples or more plates?
blocks.solution:
1. Put one apple on each plate.
2. All 5 plates now have an apple: that is 5 pairs.
3. One apple has no plate. It is left over.
4. The apples have a leftover, so there are more apples than plates, and fewer plates than apples.

Check by counting: 6 apples, 5 plates. 5 comes before 6 when we count, so 5 is fewer.

items.q: 5 cups and 5 saucers are matched one to one. Nothing is left over. What can you say?
items.a: There are the same number of cups and saucers: the groups are equal.

items.q: 7 children and 8 chairs. Each child sits on one chair. One chair is empty. Which group has fewer?
items.a: The children: there are fewer children than chairs.

items.q: Which has more: 2 elephants or 4 mice?
items.a: 4 mice. Size does not matter, only how many.

items.q: There are 4 dogs and 4 bones. Each dog gets one bone. Are there enough bones?
items.hint: Is anything left over after matching?
items.solution: Yes. 4 dogs and 4 bones make 4 pairs with nothing left over, so the groups are equal and every dog gets a bone.

items.q: There are 3 triangles and 6 squares. Which group has fewer shapes?
items.hint: Draw a line from each triangle to a square.
items.solution: After 3 lines every triangle has a partner and 3 squares are left over. So the triangles are fewer: 3 is fewer than 6.

items.q: Draw a picture with more things than this group: 6 circles. Then draw one with fewer things.
items.hint: More means some would be left over after matching with the 6 circles.
items.solution: Any picture with 7 or more things has more (for example 7 stars). Any picture with 5 or fewer things has fewer (for example 4 stars). A picture of exactly 6 things would be the same, not more or fewer.

items.q: Ben has 9 stickers and Ana has 5. What could happen to make their numbers the same?
items.hint: You could give stickers away, or get new ones.
items.solution: Ana could get 4 more stickers, so both have 9. Or Ben could give 2 to Ana, so both have 7 (9 take away 2 is 7, and 5 and 2 more is 7). Or Ben could lose 4 stickers, so both have 5.

items.q: 12 children each sit on a chair, and one chair is still empty. Are there fewer children than chairs? How do you know?
items.hint: Think of each child sitting on one chair.
items.solution: Yes. Each child is matched with a chair and one chair is left over, so there are more chairs than children: 13 chairs and 12 children.

blocks.body:
- Match one to one: the group with leftovers has more, the other has fewer.
- No leftovers on either side means the same number (equal).
- Counting gives the same answer as matching.
- Only the number of things matters, not their size.

blocks.title: Comparing numbers from 1 to 10
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to say which of two numbers from 1 to 10 is greater, and put the numbers 1 to 10 in order.

Try this first. Build three towers of cubes: one with 2 cubes, one with 6, one with 10. Which tower goes with the number 6? Count to check: the 2-tower is too short, the 10-tower is too tall.

Now build a tower for every number from 1 to 10 and stand them in a row. Each tower has one more cube than the tower before it. This is the key fact of counting: each next number name means a group that is one larger.

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(5.6, 3.2); ax = plt.gca()
for n in range(1, 11):
    x = (n - 1) * 1.0
    for k in range(n):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x, k * 0.5), 0.8, 0.5, fc='#cfe0ff', ec='blue', lw=1.0))
    ax.text(x + 0.4, -0.35, str(n), ha='center', va='top')
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 10.0); ax.set_ylim(-1.0, 5.2); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: Towers of 1 to 10 cubes in order. Each tower has one more cube than the one before.
blocks.alt: Ten towers of blue squares standing side by side like a staircase, with 1, 2, 3 up to 10 cubes. The numbers 1 to 10 are written under the towers.

blocks.title: One more, one less
blocks.body:
One more than a number is the next number when we count: one more than 5 is 6. One less than a number (one fewer) is the number just before it: one less than 5 is 4.

Adding one thing to a group gives the next number. Taking one thing away gives the number before.

blocks.title: Later in the count means more
blocks.body: Of two numbers, the one that comes later when we count is greater (it is more). The one that comes earlier is less (it is fewer). For example, 5 comes before 8, so 5 is less than 8 and 8 is greater than 5.

Count a group of 5 things. To reach 8 we must keep going: 6, 7, 8. Each extra word means one more thing. So a group of 8 is a group of 5 with 3 more things added. Matched one to one with the group of 5, the group of 8 has 3 left over, so it has more.

blocks.title: Ways to see that 7 is more than 4

items.label: Fingers
items.body: Hold up 4 fingers, then 7 fingers. Seven needs the whole first hand and two more.

items.label: The counting list
items.body: Say the numbers in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Four is said before seven, so it is less. Children use this inner list of number words to decide which is bigger.

items.label: Towers
items.body: In the row of towers, the 7-tower stands to the right of the 4-tower and is taller by 3 cubes.

items.label: Number line
items.body: A number line is a line with the numbers marked on it in order, with equal steps between them. The numbers get larger from left to right. 7 is to the right of 4, so 7 is greater.

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(5.6, 1.9); ax = plt.gca()
ax.plot([-0.4, 10.4], [0, 0], color='black', lw=1.2)
ax.annotate('', xy=(10.9, 0), xytext=(10.3, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black', lw=1.2))
for v in range(0, 11):
    ax.plot([v, v], [-0.12, 0.12], color='black', lw=1.0)
    ax.text(v, -0.3, str(v), ha='center', va='top')
for v in (4, 7):
    ax.plot([v], [0], 'o', color='blue', ms=7)
    ax.text(v, 0.3, str(v), ha='center', va='bottom', color='blue')
ax.text(5.5, 1.1, '7 is to the right of 4, so 7 is greater', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.set_xlim(-0.8, 11.2); ax.set_ylim(-1.0, 1.7); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: A number line from 0 to 10 with 4 and 7 marked by blue dots. 7 is to the right of 4, so 7 is greater than 4.
blocks.alt: A horizontal line with an arrow at the right end and ticks labelled 0 to 10. Blue dots mark 4 and 7, each labelled. Text above: 7 is to the right of 4, so 7 is greater.

blocks.title: For adults: check by counting, and check the question
blocks.body: Some children judge towers by eye and need help to see that a tower of 10 is not a tower of 6: ask them to count the 6-tower and hold it next to the number card. Some children circle the smaller number when asked for the larger. Illustrative Mathematics suggests asking what the child knows about the numbers and what they are trying to find, and inviting them to show each number with cubes. After comparing with more (8 is more than 5), ask for the same fact with less (5 is less than 8).
Put these numbers in order, starting with the least: 7, 2, 9, 4. Which is the most and which is the least?
blocks.solution:
1. Say the counting list: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
2. Of our numbers, 2 is said first, then 4, then 7, then 9.
3. So the order from least to greatest is 2, 4, 7, 9.
4. The least is 2 and the most (greatest) is 9.

Check with towers: towers of 2, 4, 7 and 9 cubes, stood in this order, get taller each time.

items.q: Which is greater, 6 or 3?
items.a: 6, because 6 comes after 3 when we count.

items.q: What is one more than 7? One less than 7?
Mai's tower has 5 cubes. How many cubes are in a tower with one fewer?
Circle the number that is more: 4 or 8.
items.hint: Which do you say later when you count?
items.solution: 8. When we count we say 4 before 8, so 8 is more.

items.q: Circle the number that is less: 5 or 9.
items.hint: Less means it comes earlier in the count.
items.solution: 5, because 5 comes before 9.

items.q: Towers of 1 to 10 cubes stand in order, but three numbers are missing: 1, 2, __, 4, 5, 6, __, 8, __, 10. Fill them in.
items.hint: Each tower is one more than the one before.
items.solution: 3, 7 and 9. One more than 2 is 3, one more than 6 is 7, one more than 8 is 9.

items.q: Show 5 and 7 in two different ways (fingers, dots, cubes). Which is more?
items.hint: Try 5 fingers on one hand and then 7 fingers.
items.solution: For example 5 fingers on one hand and 7 fingers using both hands, or 5 dots and 7 dots matched one to one. 7 is more: after matching, 2 of the 7 are left over.

items.q: Put in order from greatest to least: 3, 10, 6, 1, 8.
items.hint: Find the greatest first, then the next greatest.
items.solution: 10, 8, 6, 3, 1. In the counting list 10 comes last, then 8, then 6, then 3, and 1 comes first.

items.q: Grab a handful of beans and count them. Is your number more or less than 7? Make up a handful that is exactly one more than 7.
items.hint: Compare your count with 7 in the counting list.
items.solution: Answers depend on the handful. If you count 5, then 5 is less than 7; if you count 9, then 9 is more. A handful that is one more than 7 has 8 beans.

blocks.body:
- Each next counting number is one more than the one before.
- A number said later in the count is greater; one said earlier is less.
- One more than 5 is 6; one less than 5 is 4.
- To order numbers, follow the counting list: least first, greatest last.

blocks.title: Saying it with symbols: greater than, less than, equal to
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to read and write comparisons with the symbols $>$, $<$ and $=$.

Notice and wonder. Look at these two lines. What is the same? What is different?

$$49 > 45 \qquad 45 < 49$$

They look different, but they say the same thing about the same two numbers. The first says 49 is greater than 45. The second says 45 is less than 49.

blocks.title: The comparison symbols
blocks.body:
For two numbers $a$ and $b$ (letters standing for any numbers):

- $a > b$ is read a is greater than b.
- $a < b$ is read a is less than b.
- $a = b$ is read a is equal to b.

The open, wide side of $>$ or $<$ faces the larger number. The pointed, small side faces the smaller number. So in $8 > 3$ the wide side faces 8.

blocks.title: Ways to read a comparison

items.label: Read it aloud
items.body: Say the statement in words, left to right: 49 is greater than 45. Saying it aloud is how children test whether it is true.

items.label: Wide side, big number
items.body: The wide side of the symbol faces the larger number and the point faces the smaller one, whichever way round the numbers are written.

items.label: Left and right
items.body: On a number line, $a < b$ means $a$ is to the left of $b$, and $a > b$ means $a$ is to the right of $b$.

blocks.title: One fact, two statements
blocks.body:
Saying that $a$ is less than $b$ is the same as saying that $b$ is greater than $a$:

$$a < b \ \text{ means the same as } \ b > a$$

For example, $7 < 11$ and $11 > 7$ say the same thing.

Both statements describe the same picture: the smaller number $a$ on the left of the number line and the larger number $b$ on its right. Read from $a$, that is $a$ is less than $b$; read from $b$, that is $b$ is greater than $a$. Swapping the two numbers turns the symbol round, and its wide side still faces the larger number.
What is the greatest whole number that makes this statement true? $$\square < 35$$
blocks.solution:
1. Read it aloud: some number is less than 35.
2. Try 35: 35 is less than 35 is false, because 35 is equal to 35.
3. Try 34: 34 is less than 35 is true, since 34 comes just before 35.
4. Any number greater than 34 is 35 or more, so it is not less than 35.

So 34 is the greatest number that works. Every number from 0 to 34 also makes it true.

blocks.title: For adults: when a child writes a false statement
blocks.body: If a child writes something like $45 > 49$, do not just correct it. Illustrative Mathematics suggests asking the child to read the statement aloud and say how they could prove it is true, and then asking what other numbers would make it a true statement and how they know.

blocks.title: Words and symbols in different curricula

rows.text: Year 1 asks for the words equal to, more than, less than (fewer), most and least. The symbols $<$, $>$ and $=$ are first required in Year 2, for numbers up to 100.
Kindergarten compares in words (greater than, less than, equal to). Grade 1 records comparisons of two-digit numbers with $>$, $=$ and $<$.

England writes less than (fewer) side by side. In Illustrative Mathematics Kindergarten the question asks which group has fewer students, and the sample answer says that 5 is less than 9, without explaining the two words. Both words describe the same comparison.
England's Key Stage 3 and GCSE add $\neq$ (not equal to), $\leq$ (less than or equal to) and $\geq$ (greater than or equal to).

items.q: Read aloud: $6 < 9$.
Write $12 > 8$ the other way round.
Is $23 = 23$ true?
Write $<$, $>$ or $=$ in each blank: 7 __ 4; 3 __ 9; 8 __ 8.
items.hint: Read each statement aloud once you have chosen a symbol.
Count: which number do you say later?
items.solution: $12 > 9$, because 12 comes after 9 when we count. $15 < 18$, because 15 comes before 18.

items.q: Find a number that makes $\square > 78$ true.
items.hint: Count on from 78.
items.solution: Any number greater than 78, for example 79, 80 or 95. Check 95: 95 comes after 78 when we count, so 95 is greater than 78.

items.q: Find a number that makes $39 < \square$ true, and one that makes $13 = \square$ true.
items.hint: For the second one, how many numbers are equal to 13?
items.solution: For the first, any number greater than 39, for example 40 or 52. For the second, only 13 itself works.

items.q: What is the least whole number that makes $\square > 60$ true?
items.hint: Is 60 greater than 60?
items.solution: 61. The number 60 is equal to 60, not greater, and 61 comes just after 60.

items.q: Write two true statements about 18 and 81, one with $<$ and one with $>$.
items.hint: One fact, two statements.
items.solution: $18 < 81$ and $81 > 18$. (81 comes after 18 when we count.)

blocks.body:
- $a > b$: a is greater than b. $a < b$: a is less than b. $a = b$: a is equal to b.
- The wide side of the symbol faces the larger number.
- $a < b$ and $b > a$ say the same thing.
- Reading a statement aloud is a good test of whether it is true.

blocks.title: Two-digit numbers: compare the tens first
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to compare any two numbers up to 99 by looking at their tens and ones.

A two-digit number tells us how many tens and how many ones: 56 is 5 tens and 6 ones (see [[place-value]]).

Try this game for two players. Each player draws digit cards from 0 to 9, one at a time, and puts each card in the tens place or the ones place of their number. A card cannot be moved once placed. The greater number wins. Your partner has already put 5 in their tens place. Your number is still empty, and you draw a 6. Where should it go?

blocks.caption: 56 is 5 tens and 6 ones; 26 is 2 tens and 6 ones. Both have 6 ones, but 5 tens is more than 2 tens, so 56 > 26.
blocks.alt: Left in blue: five tall towers of ten small squares each and six single squares, labelled 56: 5 tens and 6 ones. Right in green: two towers of ten and six single squares, labelled 26: 2 tens and 6 ones.

blocks.title: Tens first, then ones
blocks.body:
To compare two two-digit numbers:

1. Compare the tens. The number with more tens is greater, whatever the ones are.
2. If the tens are the same, compare the ones. The number with more ones is greater.
3. If the tens and the ones are both the same, the numbers are equal.

A number can have at most 9 ones, because ten ones make another ten. So the ones together are always fewer than one ten.

Take a number with 5 tens. Even with the most ones it is 5 tens and 9 ones, which is 59. A number with 6 tens is at least 60. Since 59 is just before 60, every number with 5 tens is less than every number with 6 tens. The same works for any number of tens: one extra ten is worth more than any ones can make up.

So in the game the 6 should go in your tens place. Your number then has 6 tens and your partner's has 5 tens, so yours is greater whatever ones either of you draws next.

blocks.title: Ways to compare 45 and 49

items.label: Towers and cubes
items.body: Build each number with towers of ten and single cubes. Both have 4 towers. 49 has 9 single cubes and 45 has 5, so 49 is greater.

items.label: Digits by place
items.body: Compare digits in the same place. The tens digits are both 4. The ones digits are 9 and 5, and 9 is greater, so $49 > 45$.

items.label: Number line
items.body: On a number line from 40 to 50, 49 is to the right of 45, so 49 is greater.

blocks.body: Compare 72 and 78. Then compare 92 and 29. Write each answer with a symbol.
blocks.solution:
72 and 78:

1. Tens: 72 has 7 tens and 78 has 7 tens. They are the same.
2. Ones: 72 has 2 ones and 78 has 8 ones. 2 is less than 8.
3. So $72 < 78$.

92 and 29:

1. Tens: 92 has 9 tens and 29 has 2 tens. 9 tens is more.
2. We can stop: the ones do not matter.
3. So $92 > 29$, even though 29 has the bigger ones digit.

blocks.title: 17 and 71 are not the same
blocks.body: The digits 1 and 7 make 17 (1 ten and 7 ones) or 71 (7 tens and 1 one). The place of a digit decides what it is worth. When numbers are shown with cubes or drawings, look at what each part stands for (towers of ten or single cubes), not just at which part is on the left: a picture can show the ones first.

blocks.title: For adults: ordering is not the same as understanding
blocks.body: Research with Australian children in Grades 2 to 4 (Gervasoni and colleagues, 2011) found that many who could read, write and order three-digit numbers could not interpret how many each number stands for. Success at putting numbers in order may hide gaps in a child's grasp of tens and ones. The authors suggest teaching that focuses on what the numbers mean as quantities and on building a picture of the number line in the mind, not only on reading, writing and ordering numerals.

items.q: Which is greater, 38 or 52?
Which is less, 64 or 61?
items.a: 61: the tens are equal and 1 one is less than 4 ones.

items.q: Suppose your number ends up as 5 tens and 6 ones. Is it greater than 49?
items.a: Yes: your number is 56, and $56 > 49$ because 5 tens is more than 4 tens.

items.hint: Compare the tens first.
items.solution: $34 < 43$: 3 tens is less than 4 tens.

items.hint: The tens are the same, so look at the ones.
items.solution: $87 > 85$: both have 8 tens, and 7 ones is more than 5 ones.

items.q: Use the digit cards 3 and 8, each once, to make the greatest two-digit number and the least two-digit number.
items.hint: The bigger digit is worth most in the tens place.
items.solution: Greatest 83 (8 tens, 3 ones). Least 38 (3 tens, 8 ones). Check: $83 > 38$.

items.q: Find all the numbers that make $\square 4 > 64$ true, where the box is a tens digit.
items.hint: The ones are both 4, so the tens must decide.
items.solution: The tens digit must be more than 6: 74, 84 and 94. (64 itself is equal, not greater.)

items.q: Ava says 9 is greater than 10 because 9 is a bigger digit than 1. Is she right?
items.hint: How many tens does each number have?
items.solution: No. 9 has 0 tens and 9 ones; 10 has 1 ten. One ten is more than any number of ones, so $10 > 9$.

items.q: Make the statement true with a two-digit number: $47 < \square < 52$. Find every answer.
items.hint: Count on from 47 to 52.
items.solution: 48, 49, 50 and 51. They come after 47 and before 52.

blocks.body:
- A two-digit number is tens and ones.
- More tens means greater, whatever the ones.
- Same tens: the ones decide.
- The ones are always fewer than one ten (at most 9), which is why the tens come first.

blocks.title: Bigger numbers: start with the highest place
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to compare three-digit numbers and larger numbers, such as 63,951 and 630,951, using place value.

Think about this. Tyler says to compare two numbers you should start with the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. Mai says to start with the hundreds. Who is right? Test both ideas on 261 and 175, then look at 261 and 313 in the picture below.

England expects comparing and ordering up to 1,000 in Year 3, beyond 1,000 in Year 4 and to at least 1,000,000 in Year 5. In the United States this is Grade 2 (three-digit numbers) and Grade 4 (multi-digit numbers).

blocks.caption: 261 is 2 hundreds, 6 tens and 1 one; 313 is 3 hundreds, 1 ten and 3 ones. 3 hundreds is more than 2 hundreds, so 313 > 261, though 261 has more tens.
blocks.alt: Base-ten pictures. Left in blue: two large squares of a hundred small squares, six long strips of ten, and one small square. Right in green: three hundred-squares, one ten-strip and three small squares.

blocks.title: Comparing whole numbers by place value
blocks.body:
Write the numbers in the usual way, with no extra zeros at the front.

1. If one number has more digits, it is greater.
2. If they have the same number of digits, compare the digits in the same place, starting from the highest place (the left).
3. The first place where the digits differ decides: the number with the larger digit there is greater.
4. If no place differs, the numbers are equal.

Each place is worth ten of the place to its right: ten ones make a ten, ten tens make a hundred, ten hundreds make a thousand.

Look at everything below the hundreds place. It is at most 9 tens and 9 ones, which is 99, and 99 is one less than a hundred. So one extra hundred is worth more than anything the tens and ones can add. The same is true for every place: all the lower places together are at most $99\ldots9$, one less than one unit of the place above. For example

$$999 + 1 = 1000$$

This explains rule 3: the highest place that differs settles the comparison. It also explains rule 1: a number with more digits has a unit of a higher place, so a four-digit number is at least 1,000, while a three-digit number is at most 999.

So Mai is right that the hundreds come first: 313 has 3 hundreds and 261 has only 2. Tyler's idea of starting with the ones happens to give the right answer for 313 and 261 (3 ones against 1 one), but it fails on 261 and 175. The ones say 1 is less than 5, yet 261 has 2 hundreds against 1 hundred, so $261 > 175$. The ones matter only when the hundreds and tens are equal, as in 338 and 336.

blocks.title: Ways to compare three-digit numbers

items.label: Base-ten pictures
items.body: Draw hundreds as squares, tens as strips, ones as small squares. Count the hundreds first; more hundreds means a greater number. If the hundreds match, count the tens.

items.label: Digits by place
items.body: Line up hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones, and compare from the hundreds down.

items.label: Number line
items.body: Mark both numbers on a number line, for example 247 and 274 on a line from 240 to 280. The one further right is greater: $274 > 247$.

blocks.body: Compare 338 and 336. Then compare 239 and 165.
blocks.solution:
338 and 336:

1. Hundreds: 3 and 3, the same.
2. Tens: 3 and 3, the same.
3. Ones: 8 and 6. 8 is greater.
4. So $338 > 336$.

239 and 165:

1. Hundreds: 2 and 1. 2 hundreds is more.
2. Stop here. So $239 > 165$, even though 165 has more tens (6 against 3).

blocks.title: Count the tens before you trust the picture
blocks.body: A picture may not be tidied up. One picture shows 2 hundreds, 2 tens and 4 ones; another shows 1 hundred, 12 tens and 4 ones. The second looks smaller, but 12 tens is 1 hundred and 2 tens, so both show 224 and $224 = 224$. Before comparing hundreds, check whether ten or more tens (or ones) can make a new unit.

blocks.title: Bigger digits do not make a bigger number
blocks.body:
Some learners think 58,978 is greater than 547,612 because its digits look bigger (two 8s, a 9). But 58,978 has five digits and 547,612 has six. Reading the numbers aloud helps: fifty-eight thousand against five hundred forty-seven thousand. So does comparing the highest places: 58,978 has no hundred-thousands at all.

The leftmost-digit test only works when the numbers have the same number of digits. It works for 6,315 and 4,315, but not for 6,315 and 42,315: there $42,315 > 6,315$ because 42,315 has more digits.

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.0, 2.3); ax = plt.gca()
heads = ['hundred\nthousands', 'ten\nthousands', 'thousands', 'hundreds', 'tens', 'ones']
rows = [('58,978', ['', '5', '8', '9', '7', '8']), ('547,612', ['5', '4', '7', '6', '1', '2'])]
w = 1.1
for j, h in enumerate(heads):
    ax.text(1.6 + j * w + w / 2, 2.15, h, ha='center', va='center', fontsize=9)
for i, (name, ds) in enumerate(rows):
    y = 1.2 - i * 0.8
    ax.text(1.4, y, name, ha='right', va='center')
    for j, d in enumerate(ds):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((1.6 + j * w, y - 0.38), w, 0.76, fill=False, ec='black', lw=0.8))
        col = 'red' if j == 0 else 'black'
        ax.text(1.6 + j * w + w / 2, y, d if d else '(none)', ha='center', va='center', color=col if d else 'gray', fontsize=11 if d else 8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 8.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 2.6); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 58,978 and 547,612 in a place-value chart. 547,612 has a digit 5 in the hundred-thousands place and 58,978 has none there, so 547,612 > 58,978.
blocks.alt: A place-value chart with six columns headed hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. Row one, 58,978: an empty hundred-thousands box marked none, then 5, 8, 9, 7, 8. Row two, 547,612: 5 in red in the hundred-thousands box, then 4, 7, 6, 1, 2.

blocks.body: One digit is hidden in each number below, and it is the same hidden digit in both: $\square 17$ and $\square 62$. Can we tell which number is greater?
blocks.solution:
1. Both numbers have three digits (so the hidden digit is not 0), and the hundreds digit is the same (the hidden one).
2. So the hundreds do not decide. Move to the tens.
3. Tens: 1 and 6. 6 is greater.
4. So $\square 62$ is greater, whatever the hidden digit is. For example, with 4 hidden: $462 > 417$.

blocks.title: For adults: when a child says I just know
blocks.body: Learners may say they just know which number is greater, or think every digit must be compared. Illustrative Mathematics suggests asking which features of the numbers gave the clue and which digits they paid attention to, so that the place-value reason is said out loud.

items.q: Which is greater, 1,000 or 999?
items.a: 1,000: it has four digits and 999 has three.

items.q: Compare 445 and 447.
items.a: $445 < 447$: hundreds and tens match, and 5 ones is less than 7 ones.

items.q: Which place decides between 630,951 and 631,051?

items.hint: The hundreds are equal in both pairs.
items.solution: $283 > 262$ (8 tens against 6 tens). $311 < 339$ (1 ten against 3 tens).

items.q: Compare 205 and a picture showing 2 hundreds, 10 tens and 4 ones.
items.hint: Can the 10 tens make something new?
items.solution: 10 tens is 1 hundred, so the picture shows 3 hundreds and 4 ones, which is 304. Then $205 < 304$ because 2 hundreds is less than 3 hundreds.

items.q: Using each of the digits 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9 at most once, make the greatest three-digit number and the least three-digit number.
items.hint: Put the largest digits in the highest places for the greatest number.
items.solution: Greatest 976, least 236. For the greatest, the highest place gets the largest digit 9, then 7, then 6. For the least, the hundreds get the smallest digit 2, then 3, then 6.

items.q: Find one number that makes both $\square < 513$ and $\square > 479$ true.
items.hint: The number must be between 479 and 513.
items.solution: Any number from 480 to 512, for example 500. Check: $500 < 513$ and $500 > 479$.

items.q: Can one number make both $\square > 718$ and $\square < 709$ true?
items.hint: Which is greater, 718 or 709?
items.solution: No. A number greater than 718 is also greater than 709, because $709 < 718$. So it cannot be less than 709 at the same time.

items.q: Order from least to greatest: 87,696; 847,040; 84,381.
items.hint: First sort by the number of digits.
items.solution: 847,040 has six digits, so it is greatest. Of the five-digit numbers, both have 8 ten-thousands; thousands 4 against 7 gives $84,381 < 87,696$. Order: 84,381; 87,696; 847,040.

items.q: The same digit goes in both boxes: $4\square,300$ and $3\square,400$. Can the first number be less than the second?
items.hint: Which place is the highest, and what is there?
items.solution: No. Both numbers have five digits, and the ten-thousands digits are 4 and 3. Since 4 is greater, the first number is always greater, whatever the hidden digit.

blocks.body:
- More digits means a greater whole number.
- Same number of digits: compare place by place from the left.
- The first place that differs decides; lower places cannot catch up, since they add up to less than one unit of the place above.
- Tidy a picture first: ten of one unit make one of the next.
- Bigger-looking digits do not mean a bigger number; place matters.

blocks.title: Putting several numbers in order
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to put a list of numbers in order from least to greatest or from greatest to least, and show the order on a number line.

Try this first. Five numbers are 441, 418, 481, 487 and 429. Which is the greatest? Which is the least? Where would each go on a number line from 410 to 490?

To order a list, compare the numbers with the place-value rule. A good habit is to sort them first by the number of digits, then by the highest place, and keep going place by place inside each group. A number line shows the result: the numbers get larger from left to right, so the least is furthest left and the greatest furthest right (see [[number-line]]).

blocks.code:
fig = plt.gcf(); fig.set_size_inches(6.0, 1.9); ax = plt.gca()
ax.plot([408, 492], [0, 0], color='black', lw=1.2)
ax.annotate('', xy=(494, 0), xytext=(491, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='black', lw=1.2))
for v in range(410, 491):
    h = 0.16 if v % 10 == 0 else 0.07
    ax.plot([v, v], [-h, h], color='black', lw=0.9 if v % 10 == 0 else 0.6)
for v in range(410, 491, 10):
    ax.text(v, -0.3, str(v), ha='center', va='top')
pts = [(418, 0.45), (429, 0.45), (441, 0.45), (481, 0.45), (487, 0.95)]
for v, y in pts:
    ax.plot([v], [0], 'o', color='blue', ms=6)
    ax.plot([v, v], [0.08, y - 0.08], color='blue', lw=0.8)
    ax.text(v, y, str(v), ha='center', va='bottom', color='blue')
ax.text(450, 1.25, 'further right means greater', ha='center', va='bottom')
ax.set_xlim(404, 497); ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 1.65); ax.axis('off')
blocks.caption: 418, 429, 441, 481 and 487 on a number line from 410 to 490. Read from left to right they are in order from least to greatest.
blocks.alt: A horizontal number line with large ticks labelled 410, 420 and so on to 490 and small ticks for every whole number. Blue dots mark 418, 429, 441, 481 and 487, each with its label above.

blocks.body: Order 441, 418, 481, 487 and 429 from greatest to least.
blocks.solution:
1. All five numbers have 4 hundreds, so the hundreds do not help.
2. Tens: 441 has 4, 418 has 1, 481 has 8, 487 has 8, 429 has 2.
3. Largest tens first: 481 and 487 (8 tens), then 441 (4 tens), then 429 (2 tens), then 418 (1 ten).
4. 481 and 487 tie on tens; compare ones: 7 is more than 1, so 487 comes before 481.
5. Order: 487, 481, 441, 429, 418.

On the number line, reading from right to left gives the same order.

blocks.body: Video game scores: Mai 93,005; Priya 101,012; Kiran 90,298; Noah 90,056; Clare 98,032; Elena 89,100. Rank them from highest to lowest.
blocks.solution:
1. Digits: Priya's 101,012 has six digits; the others have five. Priya is first.
2. Ten-thousands: Mai, Kiran, Noah and Clare have 9; Elena has 8, so Elena is last.
3. Thousands among the 9s: Clare 8, Mai 3, Kiran 0, Noah 0. So Clare, then Mai.
4. Kiran 90,298 and Noah 90,056 tie on thousands; hundreds 2 against 0, so Kiran is ahead.
5. Ranking: Priya, Clare, Mai, Kiran, Noah, Elena.

A new score that puts a player in second place would have to lie between Clare's 98,032 and Priya's 101,012, such as 100,000.

items.q: Order 5, 50 and 15 from least to greatest.
On a number line, which is further right: 302 or 230?

items.a: 63,591 (the hundreds place decides against 63,951; 630,951 has more digits).

items.q: Order from least to greatest: 61, 16, 66, 11.
items.hint: Compare tens first.
items.solution: 11, 16, 61, 66. 11 and 16 have 1 ten (1 one against 6 ones); 61 and 66 have 6 tens.

items.q: Order from greatest to least: 909, 990, 99, 900.
items.hint: One number has fewer digits.
items.solution: 990, 909, 900, 99. 99 has two digits, so it is least. Of the rest, 990 has 9 tens; 909 and 900 have 0 tens, and 9 ones beats 0 ones.

items.q: Mark 247 and 274 on a number line from 240 to 280. Which is further right? Write the comparison.
items.hint: Both have 2 hundreds; look at the tens.
items.solution: 274 is further right (it is between 270 and 280; 247 is between 240 and 250). So $247 < 274$.

items.q: Order from least to greatest: 63,591; 630,951; 63,951; 631,051.
items.hint: Sort by number of digits first.
items.solution: 63,591; 63,951; 630,951; 631,051. The five-digit numbers come first; the hundreds (5 against 9) put 63,591 before 63,951. The six-digit numbers differ first in the thousands (0 against 1).

items.q: Write the numbers 1 to 10 that are greater than 4 and less than 8, in order.
items.hint: Count on from 4.

items.q: Make all the three-digit numbers you can with the cards 5, 7 and 3 (each once), and put them in order from least to greatest.
items.hint: There are six numbers. Start with the ones that have 3 hundreds.

blocks.body:
- To order, compare with place value: number of digits first, then the highest place, then the next.
- Least to greatest reads left to right on a number line.
- The least number is furthest left, the greatest furthest right.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
The number line turns comparing into position: greater means further right. That idea carries on when the number line grows to the left of zero. With negative numbers, $-1 < 9$ and also $-1 > -4$, because $-1$ is to the right of $-4$ (see [[number-line]]). England's Key Stage 3 asks pupils to use the number line as a model for ordering all the real numbers, including decimals and fractions ([[real-numbers]]).

Secondary school also adds three symbols: $a \neq b$ (a is not equal to b), $a \leq b$ (a is less than b or equal to it) and $a \geq b$ (a is greater than or equal to b). Statements with an unknown, such as $x + 2 < 10$, are inequalities, and finding every number that makes one true is the subject of [[solving-inequalities]]. The make-it-true puzzles on this page, such as $\square < 35$, are the first steps.

Comparing also moves into measurement: England's Year 2 asks children to compare and order lengths, masses and volumes and record the results with $>$, $<$ and $=$.
